d.title: Six components, one shared encoder, and the order is a dependency graph
d.caption: **`tok2vec` computes the token vectors every downstream component reads — shared, so the encoder runs once rather than per component**, which is why §04's timings behave the way they do. And the order is not arbitrary: **the lemmatizer needs the POS tag, which is why it runs after the tagger**, and `attribute_ruler` sits between them applying rule-based fixes over the statistical output. **Nothing here is hidden — you can print the list, reorder it, remove from it and add to it.**

items.sub: token.tag_, the fine Penn Treebank tag

d.title: Two details in one annotated sentence
d.caption: **`U.K.` survived as a single token, full stops included — the tokeniser carries exception lists for abbreviations, so it neither splits on that full stop nor treats it as a sentence boundary.** And **`$1 billion` is one entity span covering three tokens**, which is why `doc.ents` yields spans rather than tokens: an entity's boundaries do not have to line up with anything you can read off a single token.

d.title: A Token stores an index, not a string
d.caption: `token.i = 3` and `token.idx = 17`, and `doc.text[17:19]` is `'at'` — **so every attribute you read is a lookup into the parent `Doc`'s arrays, and nothing is copied.** Slicing gives a `Span`, which is likewise a pair of indices. **Which is why `doc[0].doc is doc` returns `True`**: the views keep a reference to the document, so passing a `Span` around costs nothing and **keeps the whole `Doc` alive**, which is the one practical consequence.

nodes.label: So a Span keeps the whole Doc alive

d.title: The parser and NER are the cost; everything after that is tok2vec
d.caption: **Dropping the parser and NER roughly halved the time — 0.988s to 0.550s — and dropping everything else after that bought almost nothing (0.534s), because `tok2vec` is still running and it is the shared cost underneath.** So the lever is those two components, not the component count. The second measurement compounds with it: **`nlp.pipe` on 500 documents is 2.30× faster than calling `nlp` in a loop.** And if you genuinely only want tokens, **`nlp.make_doc` skips the pipeline altogether.**

d.title: A four-line component, and the position in the list is a correctness question
d.caption: The component works on three inputs and **fails on `not good at all`, calling it positive** — which is 2.2's negation problem arriving in a custom component. The structural point is the placement: **`last=True` puts it after NER so it can read `doc.ents`; `before="ner"` would let it modify tokens the entity recogniser then sees.** And **a component needing POS tags must run after the tagger — spaCy will not stop you getting that wrong, it will hand you empty attributes.**

d.title: Two matchers, and choosing wrongly costs three orders of magnitude
d.caption: **If you know the exact strings or the exact grammatical shape you want, a matcher is faster, exact and debuggable — statistical models are not always the right tool.** The two are not interchangeable: **`Matcher` takes token patterns with attribute predicates like `POS`, so it can express *adjective followed by noun*; `PhraseMatcher` takes literal phrases only.** The next section measures what that choice costs, and the answer is three orders of magnitude.

d.title: The case is the machinery, not the model — and that cuts both ways
d.caption: **It is not that spaCy's models are the most accurate: `en_core_web_trf` is competitive, and a fine-tuned transformer will usually beat it.** The case is that **one object holds all annotations with offsets preserved, components are declarative and swappable, batching and multiprocessing are first-class, the models are versioned artefacts you pin, and it runs on CPU fast enough that per-document cost is a non-issue.** So it stops being the answer where the task is **classification or generation rather than linguistic annotation.**

nodes.label: CPU-fast: per-doc cost is a non-issue
Nor for domain-specialised NER

d.title: Where spaCy hands you one pipeline, NLTK hands you the parts
d.caption: NLTK **predates the production libraries by a decade** and is a teaching and research toolkit: **dozens of corpora, several implementations of most classical algorithms so you can compare them, and the lexical resources — which is the part with no real substitute.** WordNet, VADER's lexicon and the stopword lists exist nowhere else in this form. **And nothing ships with the package: `nltk.download('punkt')` fetches data at runtime, which is a deployment consideration rather than a detail.**

nodes.label: No real substitute for those
nodes.sub: which is why it stays installed

nodes.label: But nothing ships with the package

d.title: The sentence splitter did not break after Inc.
d.caption: Both hard cases come out right: **`Inc.` keeps its full stop as one token, and the sentence splitter still broke after `Cupertino.` rather than after `Inc.`** — that is the **Punkt** model, which is trained rather than rule-based, doing exactly what it should. Worth noting because it is the same decision 1.1's regex got wrong on `e-mailed`: **abbreviation handling is not something a character class can express.**

d.title: Three of four entities wrong, against the result that is usually quoted
d.caption: It is commonly stated that `ne_chunk` returns *Steve Jobs (PERSON)*, *Apple Inc. (ORGANIZATION)* and *Cupertino (GPE)*. **Run on NLTK 3.10.3 it splits `Steve Jobs` into two entities and labels `Apple Inc.` as PERSON** — and spaCy's small model gets all three right. Which is the honest reason NLTK is a teaching toolkit rather than a production one: **its NER chunker is a decades-old classifier that nobody has retrained, and the documented output is not what the code does.**

d.title: Twelve words chosen to expose the difference, and the verb POS does most of the work
d.caption: **`ran` is the clearest row: both stemmers and the noun lemmatiser leave it alone, and only `wordnet-v` gets `run`** — so the part-of-speech argument from 1.2 is what separates the columns, not the algorithm. **`was` splits all four: Porter mangles it to `wa`, Snowball leaves it, and the verb lemmatiser returns `be`.** And the `universal / university / universe` block is the stemmer failure mode in one line: **all three collapse to `univers`, which is three unrelated meanings in one index key.**

d.title: Eighteen senses of bank, and a similarity you can print the reason for
d.caption: **`bank` has 18 synsets and `run` has 57** — which is the sense inventory a distributional model never gives you explicitly. `path_similarity` scores two synsets by distance in the hypernym tree: **dog/cat at 0.2000 against dog/car at 0.0769.** Crude next to an embedding, **and interpretable: you can print the path — `entity → physical_entity → object → whole → living_thing → organism → animal → domestic_animal → dog` — and see exactly why.** That is the trade WordNet always offers.

d.title: The scoring function decides whether you find any collocations at all
d.caption: Same 161,600 tokens of *Emma*, two scoring functions, two completely different lists. **Raw frequency returns `to be`, `of the`, `it was` — grammar, not phrases.** PMI returns `brunswick square`, `william larkins`, `box hill`, `maple grove`: **proper nouns and place names, which is what a collocation is.** And the one junk entry is instructive: **`don t` is a tokenisation artefact, so PMI faithfully reports that the apostrophe split produced a highly-associated pair.**

d.title: Four layers, and the second one is where you work when anything goes wrong
d.caption: **`pipeline` is the fastest way to a result and the hardest to debug** — it tokenizes, runs and post-processes in one call, so a surprising output has three possible causes you cannot see. **`AutoTokenizer` + `AutoModel` is where you own the tensors**, which is why §02 and §03 work at that level. `Trainer` is the fine-tuning loop already written, and `datasets` is memory-mapped with a caching `.map`, **so it handles corpora far larger than RAM.**

items.label: pipeline(...)
items.sub: tokenize, run, post-process in one call

d.title: Three keys, and two of them are about batching rather than text
d.caption: `input_ids` is the text. **The other two exist because a model takes rectangular tensors: `token_type_ids` marks which of two segments each token belongs to — all zeros here because there is one sentence — and `attention_mask` marks which positions are real.** On a single unpadded input the mask is all ones and looks redundant, which is exactly why it gets dropped. **§03 measures what that costs.**

d.title: Cosine 1.000000 with the mask, 0.472976 without
d.caption: The same short sentence, padded to 12 and embedded two ways. **With the mask the result is identical to the unpadded version — cosine 1.000000, max absolute difference 1.9×10⁻⁶, which is float noise. Without it, cosine 0.472976 and a max difference of 6.633.** So dropping the mask does not degrade the representation slightly: **it produces a different vector, because attention distributed weight over nine padding positions.** And nothing warns you — the code runs and the shapes are right.

d.title: The task head is 1,538 parameters against 109.5 million
d.caption: **A 768×2 matrix plus two biases — 1,538 parameters — bolted onto a 109.5M encoder, which is why the two models report the same rounded parameter count.** Practically all the knowledge is in the base model, **so fine-tuning is mostly about adapting that rather than training the head**, and it is also why 3.3's `learning_rate=2e-5` matters: you are nudging 109.5M pretrained weights, not fitting 1,538 new ones.

d.title: One sentence, three token counts, three conventions
d.caption: **12 ids, 11 and 9 for the same seven words** — so a token budget computed with one tokenizer does not transfer. The conventions differ in the opposite direction too: **BERT marks continuations with `##`; RoBERTa and GPT-2 mark word-*initial* tokens with `Ġ`, a visible stand-in for a preceding space.** And **GPT-2 adds no special tokens at all, because a causal LM has no use for `[CLS]` or `[SEP]`** — which means a pipeline that slices off the first and last ids silently eats real words.

d.title: Classification reformulated as entailment, which is why it needs no labels
d.caption: For each candidate label it asks an NLI-trained model **whether the input entails the hypothesis *This example is about {label}***, then normalises the entailment scores — `travel 0.998`, `cooking 0.994`, both correct with no labelled examples. Which makes it **the right first move on a new classification problem: it gives you a working baseline in minutes and tells you whether the label set is even separable before anyone spends a week annotating.**

nodes.label: And it tells you if the labels separate

d.title: A factual probe at 0.997, and the same mechanism reading back its training data
d.caption: `Paris is the [MASK] of France` gives `capital` at **0.997** — the probe working as intended. Then the same two sentences differing by one word: **`The man worked as a [MASK]` gives `carpenter 0.097, waiter 0.052`, and `The woman worked as a [MASK]` gives `nurse 0.220, waitress 0.160, maid 0.115, prostitute 0.038`.** Note the **confidence** gap as well as the content: the female-subject distribution is sharper, so **the model is more certain about the stereotype than about the occupation.**

d.title: Four arguments, and three of them discard data quietly
d.caption: **`learning_rate=2e-5` is two orders of magnitude below training from scratch, because higher rates destroy the pretrained weights — this is the parameter to suspect first when a fine-tune fails.** The other three are about what gets thrown away: **`truncation=True` silently discards anything past the limit, and on IMDB at 256 tokens that is a substantial fraction of each review — measure how much before accepting the number.** `padding="max_length"` wastes compute that `DataCollatorWithPadding` recovers, and **`.map` caches on a hash of the function**, so re-running is free until you change it.

nodes.sub: free to re-run, recomputes on change

d.title: Seven tasks, and the pattern is that each needs a pair
d.caption: Almost no row is one metric, and the pairings are the content. **NER needs strict *and* partial F1, because 1.7 measured a one-token boundary error costing half the span score.** Summarisation and translation both pair an n-gram metric with an embedding one — ROUGE with BERTScore, BLEU with COMET — **because surface overlap and meaning overlap fail on different inputs.** And QA reports exact match alongside token F1 for the same reason.

d.title: The same predictions scored four ways, from 0.5504 to 0.9700
d.caption: 950 / 40 / 10 documents, class 0 perfect, half of class 1, **none of class 2** — and the model is a 0.97 or a 0.55 depending entirely on the averaging. **Micro equals accuracy in single-label multiclass and is dominated by the largest class. Weighted tracks accuracy closely and hides the same things.** Only **macro** exposes the failed rare class, because every class counts equally regardless of size. **And per-class is the row to always report: the averages exist to compress it, and the compression is where the information goes.**

d.title: 0.833 measured against 0.857 quoted, and the gap is a tokenisation decision
d.caption: The quoted ROUGE-1 is **0.857** and the measured value is **0.833** on the same pair of strings — a 6/7 against a 5/6, so the difference is **how many tokens the reference was split into**, not how well the system did. Which is the general warning for every number in this lesson: **a ROUGE figure is only comparable against another produced by the same tokeniser and the same stemming setting**, and papers rarely state either.

d.title: Normalisation makes three wrong-looking answers exactly right
d.caption: SQuAD-style evaluation **lowercases, strips articles and punctuation, and collapses whitespace before comparing** — so `'arthur samuel'` and `'The Arthur Samuel'` both score **exact match True**, which is the correct behaviour and surprises people. The two metrics then split on the interesting cases: **an answer that is too long and one that is too short both score EM False and F1 0.6667**, so **F1 is what distinguishes a near-miss from `'Alan Turing'` at 0.0000.**

d.title: The repeated word scores best, and the grammatical nonsense scores worst
d.caption: **`the the the the the the the the` gets perplexity 16.59 — by far the best score in the table — and `Colorless green ideas sleep furiously` gets 6413.36.** Which is exactly what perplexity measures: **how predictable the text is, not how good it is.** Degenerate repetition is maximally predictable. And **it is not comparable across models with different tokenizers**: two models scoring 20 and 25 on the same text are not ranked unless they share a vocabulary, because the per-token normalisation depends on the split.

d.title: One fixes BLEU's matching; the other abandons matching
d.caption: **METEOR keeps string comparison and widens it: stem matches, WordNet-synonym matches, and a fragmentation penalty for word order** — so *movie* can match *film* and a reordered translation is penalised explicitly rather than silently through n-gram counts. **BERTScore drops string matching entirely and greedily aligns contextual embeddings**, which is why it scores 2.4's paraphrase pair where BLEU and ROUGE score zero — **and why it needs a model, a GPU and a version pin to be reproducible.**
